name: Asymmetric cut

lead: An asymmetric cut leaves one side of the hair longer than the other, often with a diagonal line across the face. Stylists describe it as a way to frame the face, add dimension and suit round or oval faces, in anything from pixie crops to longer bobs.

It grew out of early 20th-century bob variations, was popularised in the 1960s through stylists such as Vidal Sassoon, and returned during the punk, new wave and 2000s celebrity eras. For men, it often shows up as a textured crop or fade with one side longer.

paras: Hairdressers cut the two sides to different lengths and layer precisely so the imbalance looks deliberate; styling can include a deep side part or waves. Salons commonly suggest trims every six to eight weeks to hold the shape.

The main downside is upkeep: as hair grows the contrast blurs. A miscut can be hard to even out without cutting the longer side down. Chemical or heat styling carries the usual hair-damage considerations.

angle.text: The cut changes how hair frames the face, adding an angled line and visual interest. Stylists describe it as flattering to round or oval faces, though this is styling guidance and not measured outcome.

lead: An asymmetric cut is a hairstyle with uneven lengths on either side of the head, usually with one side longer and an angle across the face that breaks left-right symmetry. It can be done short or long and on straight, wavy or curly hair [1].

People choose it to alter the visual shape of the face: the diagonal line is described as elongating and adding dimension, and it is recommended in styling guides for round and oval faces [1]. For men, the style often appears as a textured crop or a fade with one side left longer [1].

The cut's history runs through the bob. Short bobs appeared before World War I and became popular in the 1920s; stylist Vidal Sassoon revived and simplified the bob in the mid-1960s, and angled variations such as the A-line bob gained prominence in the 2000s through celebrities including Victoria Beckham [2][1].

paras: The defining feature is imbalance between the two sides, achieved with precise layering so that it looks intentional. Styling can emphasise it with a deep side part or textured waves [1].

Short bobs appeared among fashionable women before World War I, and the shingle cut was popular with 1920s flappers [2]. Sassoon's mid-1960s reinterpretation of the bob made it simpler and more geometric [2]. Asymmetric versions are credited with surging during 1980s punk and new wave, then returning in the 2000s with sleek angled bobs and again via social media in the 2010s [1].
Grokipedia also cites 17th-century accounts of Powhatan men wearing one side short and one long, though that source is AI-generated [1].
